analysis.one_liner: Pushes most people who file for bankruptcy into repayment plans so creditors collect more.
analysis.headline: Both chambers passed it by wide margins — 313-108 in the House and 83-14 in the Senate — but their two versions were never merged, and the bill died when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This omnibus bankruptcy bill would have rewritten the rules for people who cannot pay their debts. Its core is a 'means test': if a household's income clears a formula, their Chapter 7 filing (wiping out most debts) is presumed to be an 'abuse' and they are pushed into a Chapter 13 repayment plan, where a court supervises years of payments to creditors [S2][S5][S6]. It also stretches the waiting period between bankruptcy filings to eight years, requires credit counseling and a financial-management course before any discharge, and gives special bankruptcy protections to derivatives dealers and asset-backed lenders [S4][S5][S6]. The Senate version carried big riders — a minimum wage increase, small-business tax cuts, pension changes, and methamphetamine enforcement — that had little to do with bankruptcy [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, credit card issuers, and other unsecured creditors collect more from households in bankruptcy, because fewer people can erase their debts and more are locked into years of repayment. Derivatives dealers and asset-backed securitization firms gain priority protections that shield their contracts from bankruptcy courts. Credit counseling agencies gain a mandated market: filers must use an approved agency before they can even file. Small businesses gain new tax breaks, and minimum-wage workers would have gotten a raise under the Senate rider.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a formula-based presumption of 'abuse' — and dismissal or conversion — for Chapter 7 filers whose income exceeds IRS-style living standards, forcing them into Chapter 13 repayment plans they must document their way out of

Extends the waiting period between Chapter 7 discharges to eight years and between Chapter 13 discharges to five, and bars filers from discharging recent credit-card cash advances and luxury purchases
Bars anyone from filing until they complete a briefing from an approved credit counseling agency, and requires a financial-management course before any discharge is granted
Exempts swap, netting, and asset-backed securitization contracts from the bankruptcy automatic stay and from clawback by trustees, giving those creditors priority over others when a firm fails

Attaches unrelated riders in the Senate version: a minimum wage increase, small-business tax relief (higher expensing limits, self-employed health insurance deduction), pension rule changes, and expanded methamphetamine enforcement

Includes some debtor-side provisions: child support claims move to first priority, courts may cut creditors' claims 20% for refusing a reasonable repayment plan, credit card bills must carry minimum-payment warnings, and debts from violence at reproductive health clinics become nondischargeable

analysis.who_pays: Households in financial crisis. The means test measures what people 'should' be able to pay using government expense standards, not what they actually have, and escaping the presumption requires itemized documentation of special circumstances — a burden many struggling families cannot meet. Filers face mandatory counseling costs and delays, longer waits between discharges, liens on vehicles and household goods that survive bankruptcy, and a carve-out letting landlords evict during a case in many situations. Debtor-side attorneys face fee liability and penalties if a court later finds a filing was not justified.

drawbacks.text: The means test is built on IRS expense standards rather than actual circumstances, and rebutting the presumption of abuse requires itemized, documented proof of 'special circumstances' — so many people who genuinely cannot repay would be pushed into multi-year plans they ultimately fail
The credit-counseling prerequisite adds a hurdle, cost, and delay before someone can reach the protection of the bankruptcy court at all
Many filers would lose protection from eviction, because the automatic stay no longer blocks landlords in a wide set of rental cases
The Senate leadership bundled a minimum wage increase — a measure many Democrats wanted — into a creditor-friendly bankruptcy bill, forcing members to weigh one against the other

The strongest case for the bill: some filers who could realistically repay were discharging their debts, and creditors argue those losses are passed to ordinary borrowers through higher interest rates; the bill's stated aim was to restore the 'fresh start' for those who truly need it

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains here run overwhelmingly to lenders: the means test, longer discharge waits, and collateral rules exist to move money from bankrupt households to unsecured creditors, and the derivatives and securitization exemptions further favor Wall Street counterparties over other creditors. The genuine debtor-side items — child support priority, creditor-abuse penalties, disclosure warnings, the attached minimum wage increase — are real but are riders around the core transfer. The bill is also a sprawling omnibus whose minimum wage and methamphetamine titles make its bankruptcy provisions harder to evaluate on their own.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 313-108, the Senate then threw out the House text, swapped in a different bankruptcy bill's language, and passed that 83-14 — and since the two versions were never merged before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, nothing became law.

narrative.text: Rep. George Gekas introduced the Bankruptcy Reform Act in the House on February 24, 1999; it was referred to the Judiciary and Banking committees

The Judiciary Committee reported it amended on a 22-13 vote, and the House passed it on May 5, 1999, 313-108 — every voting Republican in favor (217-0), with 96 of 211 Democrats in favor and 107 opposed
On February 2, 2000, the Senate struck the House language, substituted the text of S. 625 as amended, and passed it 83-14 — 50 of 55 Republicans and 33 of 45 Democrats in favor

The Senate version added a 'needs-based' means test, mandatory credit counseling and debtor education, first-priority child support claims, penalties for creditors who refuse reasonable repayment plans, and riders on minimum wage, small-business tax relief, pensions, and methamphetamine enforcement
The Senate insisted on its amendment and requested a conference committee to reconcile the two bills, but the negotiators never reached agreement before the Congress ended on January 3, 2001

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Household debtors came out ahead in the narrow sense that the existing bankruptcy law — the more generous of the two — stayed in place. Unsecured creditors, chiefly credit card banks, failed to obtain the means test and collection rules they had pursued, and would wait five more years for a successor bill to become law.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan in both chambers but with a clear partisan gap: in the House, 217 of 222 voting Republicans backed it against 96 of 211 Democrats (107 Democrats opposed), and in the Senate it passed 83-14 with 33 of 45 Democrats joining 50 of 55 Republicans.

industries.note: The core of the bill — the means test, the eight-year wait between Chapter 7 discharges, tighter reaffirmation and collateral rules — channels more money from households in bankruptcy to unsecured lenders. Because lenders price expected recoveries into credit terms, ordinary borrowers ultimately fund the difference.

The bill makes an approved counseling briefing a mandatory first step for every filer and financial education a condition of discharge, creating a captive market standing between debtors and the courthouse.

industries.industry: Derivatives dealers and asset-backed securitization firms
industries.note: Swap, netting, and securitization contracts are exempted from the bankruptcy automatic stay and from trustee clawbacks, giving those counterparties priority when a firm fails. That protects the dealers but weakens the position of other creditors — including pension funds and insurers — left behind in a collapse.

Attorneys gain a larger compliance workload but face personal fee liability and civil penalties if a court finds a client's Chapter 7 filing was not justified, raising the cost and risk of representing struggling debtors.

The Senate version's tax title raises small-business expensing limits, allows full self-employed health insurance deductions, and extends the work opportunity credit — benefits unrelated to the bankruptcy core.
